_note: Curated verified figures for the proof visuals. Derived 2026-09-15 from the private, hash-checked evidence package (kept in homelabai). Only the specific values the marketing needs are baked in here; the raw package, report, and audits are NOT published.

comparisons.title: Periodic C2 callback

suricata.verdict: 17 flow rows for the host, 0 alerts — nothing flagged

cernity.verdict: one C2-beacon finding with the measured cadence

comparisons.takeaway: Suricata logged the callbacks but raised no alert. Cernity derived the 5-second cadence and named it C2.

comparisons.title: Internal fan-out

suricata.verdict: 48 flow rows, 0 alerts — connections scattered, unlinked

comparisons.takeaway: The analyst would have to aggregate 48 connections by hand. Cernity delivered the fan-out as a single lead.

comparisons.title: Repeated signature, consolidated

suricata.verdict: 45 repeating alert records for one incident

comparisons.takeaway: Here Suricata does classify the threat — and fires it 45 times. Cernity keeps it as one tracked incident.

comparisons.title: Distributed low-and-slow transfer

suricata.verdict: 44 TCP stream-anomaly alerts on the pair — none says 'exfil'

cernity.verdict: one data-exfiltration lead: 5.93 MB across 11 flows

comparisons.takeaway: Suricata's alerts were protocol noise, not a data-theft signal. Cernity summed the transfer and tagged exfiltration.

caveat.title: Honest limits
points: Cernity is not free of false leads: on a benign transfer in the same test its beacon detector raised two c2 leads that were not malicious.
These are synthetic, single-host scenarios that demonstrate the mechanism — not a population precision/recall study.
On threats Suricata already signatures, both catch it; Cernity's edge there is consolidation and enrichment.
No analyst-workload or resource-cost figure is claimed here.
